plan.chapter_thesis: Nanofabrication processes impose strict tolerance thresholds and introduce structural disorder that systematically degrade holographic fidelity below theoretical design predictions, while scalable manufacturing strategies capable of producing meter-scale metasurfaces remain largely unvalidated compared to lab-scale demonstrations.
plan.reader_takeaway: The transition from computational inverse design to physical metasurface holograms is bottlenecked by fabrication-induced disorder and the lack of validated scalable manufacturing techniques, creating a significant gap between simulated performance and experimental reality.

argument_sequence.purpose: Establish the context that inverse design generates complex geometries requiring high-precision fabrication, setting the stage for the fabrication challenge.
Define the current standard research-scale fabrication techniques (EBL/FIB) and their inherent throughput limitations.
Argue that the translation from idealized design to physical structure introduces specific structural disorders (sidewall angle, roughness) that degrade performance.
Highlight the mismatch between algorithmic outputs and physical realizability due to fabrication constraints.
Introduce scalable manufacturing proposals (NIL, roll-to-roll) as the proposed solution to throughput bottlenecks.
Conclude that despite proposals, scalable methods lack validation for maintaining nanometer-scale fidelity at meter-scales, reinforcing the central thesis.

terminology_rows.note: High-resolution serial writing technique used for research-scale metasurfaces; limited by low throughput.
Deviations including sidewall angles, feature roughness, and placement errors that degrade optical performance.
Scalable parallel patterning technique proposed to overcome EBL throughput limits; fidelity at large scales remains unvalidated.
Computational optimization of nanostructure geometry to achieve target wavefront control, often generating complex non-intuitive shapes.

explanation_block_rows.title: From Complex Designs to Fabrication Demands
explanation_block_rows.goal: Establish that modern inverse design algorithms generate highly complex geometric profiles that necessitate high-precision nanofabrication, creating an immediate dependency on fabrication capabilities.

explanation_block_rows.title: The Research-Scale Bottleneck: EBL and FIB
explanation_block_rows.goal: Describe the dominance of electron-beam lithography and focused ion beam writing in current research, emphasizing their high resolution but critical limitation in serial processing throughput.

explanation_block_rows.title: Fabrication-Induced Structural Disorder
explanation_block_rows.goal: Detail how the physical realization of designs introduces systematic errors such as sidewall deviations and surface roughness, which directly reduce diffraction efficiency and image quality below theoretical predictions.

explanation_block_rows.title: The Realizability Gap
explanation_block_rows.goal: Explain the fundamental mismatch where inverse design algorithms often propose structures that are physically unrealizable or unstable under current fabrication constraints.

explanation_block_rows.title: Proposed Scalable Manufacturing Pathways
explanation_block_rows.goal: Introduce nanoimprint lithography and roll-to-roll processing as the primary candidates for scaling up production, outlining their theoretical advantages in throughput.

explanation_block_rows.title: The Validation Deficit at Scale
explanation_block_rows.goal: Conclude that current evidence heavily favors computational design over experimental validation of scalable processes, leaving the fidelity of meter-scale holographic metasurfaces as an open and critical challenge.
